source_text: Μηδαμῶς γὰρ πλέον τι ὠφελουμένου τοῦ γινώσκοντος τὰ αὐτῷ συμβησόμενα παρὰ τὸν βίον καταθύμια· θῶμεν γὰρ τοῦτο· ὅμως δὲ καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων περιεργίᾳ ἐπιτεχνᾶται, ὡς καὶ τὰ μετὰ θάνατόν τινος ἑκάστου ἐσόμενα, πολυπραγμονεῖν τε καὶ δοκεῖν εἰδέναι. Μνήμη δὲ ἀγαθὴ ψυχῇ προσηνεστέρα, ἤπερ σώματι ἔλαιον· καὶ βίου ἔξοδος, ἀμείνων γενέσεως· καὶ αἱρετώτερον πενθεῖν, ἢ κωμάζειν, καὶ τὸ παρεῖναι τοῖς λυπουμένοις, ἢ τοῖς μεθυσκομένοις. Ἔστι γὰρ οὕτω, λαβόντα τινὰ τοῦ βίου τέλος μὴ εὐλαβηθῆναι περὶ τῶν ἀμφ᾽ αὐτόν. Γέλωτος δὲ θυμὸς ἔμφρων προτιμότερος· αὐστηρᾷ γὰρ διαθέσει προσώπου, κατορθοῦται ψυχή. Αἱ μὲν τοίνυν τῶν σοφῶν ψυχαὶ, σκυθρωπάζουσι καὶ συστέλλονται, αἱ δὲ τῶν ἀφρόνων ἐπαιρόμεναι διαχέονται. Πολὺ δέ ἐστιν εὐκταιότερον ἐπίπληξιν σοφοῦ ἑνὸς δέξασθαι, ἢ ὅλου χοροῦ ἀνθρώπων φαύλων καὶ δυστήνων ᾀδόντων γενέσθαι ἀκροατήν. Τῶν γὰρ ἀφρόνων ἀνθρώπων ὁ γέλως, ἀκανθῶν πολλῶν λάβρῳ πυρὶ καιομένων ἤχῳ προσέοικεν. Ἄθλιον δὲ καὶ τοῦτο, κακόν γε μὴν μέγιστον ἡ συκοφαντία· αὕτη γὰρ σοφῶν ἐπιβουλεύει ψυχαῖς, καὶ ἐπιχειρεῖ διαφθείρειν τὴν γενναίαν ἔνστασιν τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Λόγων δὲ οὐκ ἀρχόμενον, ἀλλὰ παυόμενον ἐπαινεῖν προσήκει, καὶ τὸ μέτριον ἦθος ἀποδέχεσθαι, καὶ μὴ τὸ μετεωριζόμενον καὶ τετυφωμένον. Πάνυ δὲ χρὴ θυμοῦ φείδεσθαι, καὶ μὴ εἰς ὀργὴν προχείρως καταφέρεσθαι, ᾗτινι ἄφρονες δουλεύουσιν.
thought_title: Mourning and rebuke teach more than laughter
orientation: Mourning, rebuke and a sober mind teach more than laughter and revelry.
pass_a_gloss: For the one knowing the agreeable things that will happen to him during life being in no way benefited more, for let us grant this; yet by the curiosity of men it is contrived both to busy oneself about the things to be after the death of each one and to seem to know. A good memory is gentler to soul than oil to body; and exit of life better than birth; and more to be chosen to mourn than to revel, and to be present with those grieving than with those getting drunk. For it is thus: someone having received the end of life not to be anxious about things around him. Prudent anger more preferable than laughter; for by stern disposition of face the soul is set right. The souls of the wise are sullen-faced and contract; those of fools, being lifted up, are diffused. Much more desirable to receive the rebuke of one wise man than to become hearer of a whole chorus of base and wretched men singing. For the laughter of foolish men resembles the noise of many thorns burning in fierce fire. Wretched also this, greatest evil indeed false accusation: for it plots against souls of the wise and attempts to destroy the noble firmness of the good. It is fitting to praise [one] not beginning but ceasing of words, and to accept the moderate character, and not the lifted-up and conceited. One must greatly spare anger and not be carried down readily into wrath, which fools serve as slaves.

pass_b_english: A man who knows the pleasant things that will befall him in life gains nothing more by it, even if we grant that he knows them; and yet human curiosity still contrives to pry into what will happen even after each person's death, and to think it knows (Ecclesiastes 6:12). A good remembrance is sweeter to the soul than oil to the body, and the departure from life is better than birth (Ecclesiastes 7:1). It is a better choice to mourn than to revel, and to be with those who grieve rather than with those who are getting drunk (Ecclesiastes 7:2). For so it is: when someone has come to the end of life, he has no anxiety about the things around him.

Sensible anger is to be preferred to laughter, for by a stern look on the face the soul is set right (Ecclesiastes 7:3). So the souls of the wise are grave and hold themselves in, while the souls of fools are puffed up and run loose (Ecclesiastes 7:4). It is far more to be wished for to receive the rebuke of one wise man than to listen to a whole chorus of base and wretched men singing (Ecclesiastes 7:5). For the laughter of foolish men is like the crackling of many thorns burning in a fierce fire (Ecclesiastes 7:6). This too is wretched, and indeed a very great evil: false accusation. It plots against the souls of the wise and tries to destroy the noble steadfastness of the good (Ecclesiastes 7:7). One should praise a speaker not as he begins his words but as he ends them, and welcome a modest character rather than one that is lofty and puffed up (Ecclesiastes 7:8). One must by all means keep anger in check and not be carried away readily into wrath, which fools serve as slaves (Ecclesiastes 7:9).
notes: Gregory's chapter 7 opens with his paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 6:12 (same numbering in English and LXX); the rest follows 7:1-9 with the same numbering. Read πλέον τι with the 1622 print (source row note). The first sentence is a genitive absolute with a concession ('let us grant this'); the English joins it to the main clause. 'When someone has come to the end of life, he has no anxiety about the things around him' renders the obscure Ἔστι γὰρ οὕτω, λαβόντα τινὰ τοῦ βίου τέλος μὴ εὐλαβηθῆναι περὶ τῶν ἀμφ᾽ αὐτόν; it may instead mean that one who has taken the end of life to heart in this way is not anxious about his surroundings. 'Sensible anger' renders θυμὸς ἔμφρων, following LXX 7:3 θυμός. 'A good remembrance' renders μνήμη ἀγαθή where the Hebrew and LXX have 'a good name'. 'Praise a speaker not as he begins his words but as he ends them' takes the accusative participles as referring to a person, with λόγων governed by the verbs of beginning and ending (LXX 7:8 'better is the end of words than their beginning'). Review check: the 1622 Latin (p. 87 D) reads the obscure sentence the same way ('Sic enim se res habet, quod si quis hunc vitae finem nactus fuerit, de his, quae circa se sunt, nec timore nec sollicitudine afficiatur').
